Hundreds of millions of people this year have been exposed to unbearable extreme heat, whilst the catastrophic ice and rock collapse and flash floods in Nepal highlighted the compound risks facing communities in fragile, warming high-mountain terrain.” Forecasts underpinned by sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever to monitor our rapidly changing climate and help navigate the increasing risks to societies and economies. The good news is that the number of countries reporting the existence of multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWSs) has increased from 56 in 2015 to 136 in 2025, according to the report. The WMO State of the Climate 2026 Update was released on the first day of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as an authoritative, science-based report. It includes data – where available – up to September 2026 and therefore does not reflect the most recent impacts of El Niño. The final State of the Global Climate 2026 report will be issued in March 2027, incorporating scientific contributions from dozens of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, regional climate centres, United Nations partners and experts from the WMO community. Highlights Global temperature: The global mean near-surface temperature anomaly averaged from January to September 2026 (1.47 °C ± 0.13 °C above the 1850–1900 average) is comparable to the whole-year averages for 2025 (1.43 °C) and 2023 (1.46 °C) and lower than the 2024 record (1.55 °C). Extreme events impacted lives and livelihoods, undermined food security, deepened poverty and contributed to displacement across multiple regions. The European heatwaves, drought and wildfires led to more than 30,000 excess deaths, according to preliminary estimates, with national temperature records in at least eight countries, and major impacts on agriculture, energy and transport. An estimated 146.5 million people in India were exposed to extreme heat in an April 2026 heatwave. The Himalayan glacier collapse and catastrophic downstream flash flood in late August killed more than 1,300 people and had a massive impact on Nepal’s economy. Tropical cyclones caused devastation and loss of life in many countries. The current El Niño is expected to act as a risk multiplier for health. Increased heat, drought and heavy rainfall can contribute to heat-related illness and mortality, wildfire smoke and poor air quality, malnutrition and food insecurity, injuries, and changing risks of water- and vector-borne diseases such as cholera, malaria and dengue. The World Health Organization (WHO) has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts as a health emergency. El Niño is already increasing risks for agriculture in key seasons and production systems, especially in areas where there is high food insecurity and heavy reliance on rainfed agriculture. Notes to Editors The nine global temperature datasets are: Berkeley Earth, CMA-GMST, CMST, DCENT-I, ERA5, GISTEMP, HadCRUT5, JRA-3Q, and NOAAGlobalTemp. This year’s report is accompanied by a new interactive online platform where users can explore the data behind the report, learn more about the methodologies, combine maps of climate data and explore El Niño. The platform is currently in beta, and user feedback is encouraged to support its further development. The World Meteorological Organization is the United Nations System’s authoritative voice on Weather, Climate and Water. h a very strong El Niño event set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). It highlights the knock-on risks to the environment, economy, and everyday life. Key messages 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record El Niño turns up the heat and multiplies risks Sea level and ocean heat are at record high levels Extreme weather has massive economic and human cost Forecasts and warnings, underpinned by sustained observations, are vital Share: WMO 2027 Calendar Competition - Gaël Handschin The WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December. Earth’s energy imbalance is rising and the earth system is accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat and 2026 is on track to be the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth.
